Sub-metanalyses A total of 25 contingency tables from the 12 studies included were subjected to a sub-meta-analysis based on study design ( Supplementary Table 2 ), number of participating centers ( Supplementary Table 3 ), population age group ( Supplementary Table 4 ), and model stage ( Supplementary Table 5 ). The common effect model indicated higher heterogeneity when analyzing retrospective ( I 2 = 90.3%–99.1%) versus prospective studies ( I 2 = 76.5%–91.8%), multicentric ( I 2 = 85%–98.7%) versus single or bicentric ( I 2 = 48.7%–84.4%), pediatrics ( I 2 = 92%–99.4%) versus adults ( I 2 = 71.6 to 88.1%). Heterogeneity also decreased from training ( I 2 = 90.2%–99.6%) to testing ( I 2 = 82.9%–94.2%), and then to validation ( I 2 = 76.5%–88.2%) stage. The common effect model demonstrated that AI models performed significantly better in prospective versus retrospective studies, in terms of sensitivity (0.98 vs 0.92; P < .0001), NPV (0.93 vs 0.82; P < .001), observed agreement (0.93 vs 0.88; P < .0001), and F1 score (0.95 vs 0.90; P < .0001). Single or bicenter studies also demonstrated better performance than multicentric in terms of specificity (0.97 vs 0.89; P < .0001) and NPV (0.94 vs 0.86; P < .0001). Furthermore, in subanalyses between adults versus pediatrics, AI models performed significantly better in adult populations for most performance metrics: sensitivity (0.97 vs 0.77; P < .0001), specificity (0.94 vs 0.80; P < .001), NPV (0.94 vs 0.52; P < .001), observed agreement (0.93 vs 0.74; P < .0001), and F1 score (0.94 vs 0.82; P < .0001). During the model development from training to validation, notable improvements were observed in most performance measures: sensitivity (0.92 vs 0.97; P < .0001), specificity (0.86 vs 0.96; P < .0001), NPV (0.63 vs 0.95; P < .0001), observed agreement (0.87 vs 0.95; P < .0001), and F1 score (0.91 vs 0.96; P < .0001). When adjusted to the random effects model, AI models performed significantly better in prospective versus retrospective studies in terms of specificity (0.91 vs 0.82; P = .03). Single or bicenter studies demonstrated better performance than multicentric in terms of specificity (0.94 vs 0.84; P < .0001) and observed agreement (0.90 vs 0.83; P = .03). Furthermore, in subanalyses between adults versus pediatrics, AI models confirmed better performance in adults for specificity (0.90 vs 0.72; P = .03) and observed agreement (0.90 vs 0.69; P = .02). No significant differences were found in the subanalysis of the other aforementioned parameters. 3.4.2. Meta-regression These sub-meta-analysis findings were supported by the meta-regression results ( Table 3 ). According to the meta-regression, pediatric AI models showed significantly lower diagnostic performance across all statistical measures compared to adult AI models, with the exception of PPV: sensitivity lower than 0.24 (−0.35, −0.12; P < .001), specificity lower than 0.21 (−0.33, −0.09; P = .0008), NPV lower than 0.49 (−0.71, −0.26; P < .001), observed agreement lower than 0.28 (−0.38, −0.17; P < .001) and F1 score lower than 0.19 (−0.30, −0.09; P = .0002) ( Table 3 ). 4. Discussion To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic review, meta-analysis, and meta-regression focused on evaluating AI models for assessing histological remission in UC and comparing digital pathology-based algorithms with pathologists. Despite the predictable substantial heterogeneity, our analysis revealed considerable AI diagnostic performance nearly comparable to that of pathologists, with nonsignificant differences in specificity, observed agreement, and F1 score. However, they outperformed AI in sensitivity and NPV. Our results highlight the significant potential of AI in the field of digital pathology for IBD. AI has emerged as a valuable tool for precise and efficient disease assessment, crucial for clinical trials and routine clinical practice. In clinical trials, AI-enhanced digital pathology can standardize and expedite slide evaluations, reducing costs, time, and human effort. 24 Furthermore, AI can address the challenges of intra- and interobserver variability, providing an accurate and objective assessment of the disease and contributing to consistent and reliable central read-outs in clinical trials. Similarly, AI can support pathologists in clinical practice by offering rapid and accurate disease assessment, thereby improving patient management. 25 Notably, we developed the first convolutional neural network that accurately predicts histological remission and long-term outcomes in UC patients based solely on the presence or absence of neutrophils. 13 , 16 Hence, AI can potentially guide therapeutic decision-making, paving the way for precision histology assessment. One of the key strengths of AI models lies in their ability to assess disease activity accurately without relying on pathologists. Our meta-analysis supports this, showing that AI can achieve diagnostic performance comparable to that of pathologists. This capability is particularly valuable in clinical settings where pathologists with adequate expertise are not available, as AI can provide a more reliable and standardized alternative to nonexpert assessment. Additionally, AI tools offer significant educational benefits by highlighting algorithmically identified histological features, which can enhance diagnostic skills and improve consistency across various levels of expertise. 31 However, AI models still require refinement, 32 as evidenced by the significantly higher sensitivity and NPV observed in pathologists, confirmed at pairwise comparisons. This disparity likely stems from the complexity of IBD pathology, which involves diverse patterns and subtle inflammation that may be challenging for AI to detect. To address this, AI models need to be trained with diverse and high-quality prospective data that encompasses the full range of histological features necessary for accurate disease assessment. Furthermore, improving AI sensitivity can be achieved by refining algorithms and implementing more advanced AI architectures capable of capturing complex patterns in histological slides. Indeed, we have recently proposed an innovative active learning-based iterative framework that showed promise in standardizing digital tissue annotation, alleviating the burden of WSI labeling, and improving disease assessment. 33 Besides, adopting a comprehensive, multimodal approach integrating clinical, endoscopic, and OMIC data with histology, referred to as the “endo-histo-OMIC” approach, could enhance AI performance. 11 This multisource integrated strategy can potentially improve disease assessment and prediction of clinical outcomes and response to therapy. Finally, it is essential to emphasize that while AI is a valuable tool for supporting pathologists, it cannot fully replace human expertise. Therefore, integrating AI within a framework guided and supervised by skilled pathologists remains crucial. This meta-analysis suffers from some limitations. The main concern is the substantial heterogeneity in AI performance metrics observed across the included studies. This variability can be attributed to several factors, elucidated by our sub-meta-analyses and meta-regressions. First, study design plays a crucial role in influencing AI performance. Our results suggest prospective studies have lower heterogeneity than retrospective studies, as they benefit from more controlled conditions and standardized procedures, likely contributing to more consistent and reliable performance metrics. Similarly, multicentric studies demonstrated greater heterogeneity than single or bicentric studies. This is likely due to differences in data quality and standardization practices across various locations. Nonetheless, the training, testing, and validation of AI models in a multicentric context are still useful in overcoming overfitting. Population demographics also impact AI performance, with models performing better and showing less heterogeneity in adults than in pediatric populations. This may be due to the distinct pathological features seen in children and the less comprehensive training data available for pediatric cases. 34 , 35 The development stage of the AI model—training, validation, or testing—further influences both performance and heterogeneity. Our findings suggest that the training stage was associated with higher heterogeneity and lower performance. This confirms the importance of rigorous and standardized methodology potentially leading to improve the AI development process and its accuracy for patient diagnosis and outcomes. Ensuring comprehensive testing and thorough validation is crucial for enhancing the generalizability and reliability of AI models to be successfully implemented and adopted. Additionally, the comparison of different AI models influences the heterogeneity of the study. The development of AI histology models must consider the standardization of processed WSI by color, resolution, and size, to reduce the variability of AI models’ performance. Another limitation is that only a minority of studies involved GI pathologist assessment, and some studies relied only on isolated morphological criteria rather than validated scores for predicting histological remission. Therefore, more robust and refined AI model studies should be considered to confirm these results and derive conclusive comparison data. Finally, the absence of performance metrics for non-GI pathologists in the literature is notable, as it hindered our ability to perform a network meta-analysis. Such an analysis is essential for assessing whether AI models are at least as effective as human pathologists, thereby validating their practical applicability and usefulness, especially within the broader pathologist community. In conclusion, our systematic review, meta-analysis, and meta-regression highlight AI’s promising potential in accurately assessing histological remission, positioning it as a valuable tool for enhancing clinical trials and IBD patient management. This prompts future research aimed at refining AI histology models to improve their performance and align more closely with pathologists. Additionally, there is a need for more standardized, large-scale studies, including randomized trials, to minimize heterogeneity and validate these preliminary findings, thereby facilitating the integration of AI into clinical practice. documents.title: Mechanistic investigation and the optimal dose based on baicalin in the treatment of ulcerative colitis-A preclinical systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a type of inflammatory bowel disease, and current treatments often fall short, necessitating new therapeutic options. Baicalin shows therapeutic promise in UC animal models, but a systematic review is needed.
METHODS: A systematic search was conducted across databases including PubMed, EBSCO, Web of Science, and Science Direct, up to March 2024, identifying randomized controlled trials (RCTs) examining baicalin's impact on UC in animal models. Seventeen studies were selected through manual screening. Meta-analyses and subgroup analyses utilized Rev Man 5.3 and Stata 15.0 software to assess symptom improvement.
RESULTS: From 1304 citations, 17 were analyzed. Baicalin significantly modulated various biomarkers: HCS (SMD = -3.91), DAI (MD = -2.75), spleen index (MD = -12.76), MDA (SMD = -3.88), IL-6 (SMD = -10.59), IL-1β (SMD = -3.98), TNF-α (SMD = -8.05), NF-κB (SMD = -5.46), TLR4 (MD = -0.38), RORγ (MD = -0.89), MCP-1 (MD = -153.25), MPO (SMD = -7.34), Caspase-9 (MD = -0.93), Caspase-3 (MD = -0.45), FasL (MD = -1.20)) and enhanced BWC (MD = 0.06), CL (MD = 1.39), ZO-1 (MD = 0.44), SOD (SMD = 3.04), IL-10 mRNA (MD = 3.14), and FOXP3 (MD = 0.45) levels. Baicalin's actions may involve the PI3K/AKT, TLR4/NF-κB, IKK/IKB, Bcl-2/Bax, Th17/Treg, and TLRs/MyD88 pathways. Optimal therapeutic outcomes were predicted at dosages of 60-150 mg/kg over 10-14 weeks.
CONCLUSION: Baicalin demonstrates a multifaceted therapeutic potential in UC, attributed to its anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, anti-apoptotic, and intestinal barrier repair properties. While higher doses and longer treatments appear beneficial, further research, particularly human clinical trials, is necessary to verify its effectiveness and safety in people.

While higher doses and longer treatments appear beneficial, further research, particularly human clinical trials, is necessary to verify its effectiveness and safety in people.

Recognized globally due to its incrementally rising incidence [ 2 ], UC is characterized by spontaneous, chronic, and recurrent inflammation of the colon, presenting symptoms such as bloody stools and chronic pain [ 3 , 4 ]. The etiology of UC remains elusive; however, current research indicates that a combination of mucosal barrier defects, genetic predisposition, and alterations in the intestinal microbiota may contribute to its pathogenesis [ 5 , 6 ]. Traditional treatments for IBD have focused on managing the immune response via glucocorticosteroids, aminosalicylates, and immunosuppressants [ 7 ]. A study demonstrated that 15% of patients experienced adverse effects following 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA) treatment, with the primary adverse effects including exacerbation of ulcerative colitis (UC), diarrhea, headache, nausea, vomiting, and rash. Three classes of biologic agents have shown efficacy in the treatment of UC: anti-tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) antibodies, anti-integrin α4β7 agents, and Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors. However, due to their high cost and the partial response in some patients, a significant number of individuals continue to endure numerous symptoms, contributing to both physical and psychological burdens associated with the disease. Given the limited efficacy, variable patient responses, and significant adverse effects associated with these medications, there has been a push to explore novel therapeutic strategies [ 8 – 10 ]. The discovery of therapeutic agents that are both highly effective and have minimal side effects remains a challenging aspect of treating Ulcerative Colitis (UC). Natural products and their derivatives have garnered significant interest within the pharmaceutical industry, leading to numerous scientific investigations. Baicalin (C 21 H 18 O 11 ), a flavonoid compound extracted from the root of Scutellaria baicalensis Georgi (family Labiatae), exhibits notable biological activities including antibacterial, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, antiviral effects, and offers protection to the liver and nervous system [ 11 ], alongside potent immunomodulatory properties [ 12 ]. Importantly, baicalin has been reported to modulate key signaling pathways implicated in UC pathogenesis, such as the NF-κB and PI3K/AKT pathways. NF-κB plays a pivotal role in driving inflammation by promoting the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β), while the PI3K/AKT pathway regulates apoptosis and cellular survival. By inhibiting NF-κB phosphorylation and reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine levels, baicalin may mitigate inflammation. Concurrently, baicalin’s ability to modulate the PI3K/AKT pathway, enhancing Bcl-2 expression and suppressing caspase activity, suggests its potential to maintain intestinal barrier integrity and reduce epithelial cell apoptosis. These mechanisms position baicalin as a promising therapeutic agent for UC. In China, baicalin capsules are extensively utilized as a therapeutic agent in the management of hepatitis. This study aims to furnish empirical evidence to support the broader application of these capsules. Although animal studies have demonstrated baicalin’s therapeutic potential for UC, meta-analyses of preclinical studies have yet to confirm its efficacy in UC treatment. This study, therefore, systematically examines these animal experiments to assess baicalin’s therapeutic impact, specifically focusing on its effects on Disease Activity Index (DAI), Body Weight Change (BWC), Colon Length (CL), Histological Score (HCS), and cytokine levels such as Interleukin 10 (IL-10), Interleukin 6 (IL-6), and Tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α), among other indices, in UC model animals. Baicalin’s therapeutic potential in UC, as demonstrated in animal models, is supported by mechanisms such as NF-κB signaling inhibition, reduction of oxidative stress, and modulation of cytokine profiles, which are also central to human UC pathogenesis (e.g., IL-6, TNF-α) [ 7 ]. This concordance between animal and human mechanisms suggests a strong basis for translational research. However, interspecies differences in metabolism, pharmacokinetics, and side effect profiles pose challenges. For instance, humans exhibit slower drug clearance rates and differing immune responses, which may influence baicalin’s efficacy and safety [ 13 ]. Addressing these gaps will require targeted pharmacokinetic studies and early-phase clinical trials to assess baicalin’s viability as a therapeutic agent for UC. This analysis aims to lay the groundwork for future clinical trials and product development, striving to furnish robust evidence-based support for baicalin’s clinical application. Materials and methods This study aimed to elucidate the impact of baicalin on UC in preclinical trials through a meta-analysis, adhering to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines [ 14 ] [ID: CRD42024527843]. Search Strategy We conducted a comprehensive search across four databases—PubMed, EBSCO, Web of Science, and Science Direct—to collate literature on preclinical studies evaluating baicalin’s effect on UC. The search, completed up to March 5, 2024, aimed to encompass a broad range of research by discussing and refining the search methodology collaboratively among study participants. Ultimately, a strategy integrating both disease and treatment terms was employed. For instance, in PubMed, the search utilized MeSH terms with combinations of “((((Baicalein) OR (baicalin)) OR (wogonoside)) OR (wogonin)) AND (((((Colitis Gravis) OR ((ulcerative colitis) OR (Idiopathic Proctocolitis))) OR (Inflammatory Bowel Disease)) OR (Ulcerative Colitis Type))”. The primary search strategy specifically targeted animal studies to ensure that the conclusions drawn from this systematic review and meta-analysis are based on preclinical models rather than clinical observations in humans. No language restrictions were imposed during the literature search. Detailed search strategies employed for each database are summarized in Supplementary Table 1. Inclusion and exclusion criteria Inclusion Criteria: Results from published studies. Studies with distinct treatment and control groups. Research objects: UC animal model, no limitations on the method of animal modeling, species, gender, or sample size. Treatment exclusively with baicalin in experimental groups; model groups served as vectors or control. Availability of all necessary experimental data. Exclusion Criteria: Reviews, case reports, conferences, case reports, clinical studies, network pharmacology and in vitro experiments. Studies not pertinent to UC. Duplicate literature. Studies lacking experimental details. Studies with significant experimental data bias. Studies not available in full text. Data extraction Two authors independently extracted data, including the authors and publication year; species, sex, weight range, and sample size of the animals; the modeling methodology for UC; details of interventions, including the period and dosage; and the types of anaesthetic drugs used. Outcome measures included HCS, BWC, CL, DAI, levels of IL-6, IL-1β, mRNA expressions of IL-10 and IL-6, TNF-α and its mRNA expression, MPO, MDA, SOD, NF-κB, caspase-9, ZO-1, caspase-3, TLR4, IL-17 mRNA, FOXP3, FasL, RORγt, MCP-1, and index of spleen (Supplementary Table 2). Any discrepancies in data extraction were resolved by consulting the corresponding author, who provided oversight to ensure unbiased and accurate results. For experiments with multiple groups, the group receiving the highest dose was chosen. Data were recorded at the final time point if presented at several intervals. Data in graphs were obtained directly from authors or extracted using GetData software. Standard errors (SEM) were converted to standard deviations (SD) using the formula SD = SEM × √N [ 15 ]. Risk of bias assessment The risk of bias was independently evaluated by two authors using the 10-item scale bias tool provided by the SYRCLE (Centre for Risk Assessment in Animal Experiments) [ 16 ]. The quality of the selected literature on baicalin for UC was assessed across several domains: selection bias, performance bias, detection bias, attrition bias, reporting bias, and other potential biases. Each domain was rated as having a low, high, or unclear risk based on predefined criteria, and a risk of bias map was constructed. Discrepancies in the assessment were resolved through discussion with the corresponding authors. Data analysis Data analysis was conducted using STATA version 15.0 (Stata Corp., USA) and RevMan (version 5.3). Continuous outcomes in same units across studies, such as body weight change, colon length, and histological score, were expressed as mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The standardized mean difference (SMD) was employed for outcomes measured in varying units across studies, such as interleukin-6 levels. We used either a fixed-effects(I 2 ≤ 50%) or a random-effects(I 2 > 50%) model to pool results, based on whether MD or SMD was calculated, considering P < 0.05 as statistically significant. Heterogeneity was assessed using the Chi-square and I 2 tests, with sensitivity or subgroup analyses conducted for I 2 values over 50% to explore heterogeneity sources. Subgroup analysis and sensitivity analyses Subgroup analyses were performed based on animal species (mice and rats), drug dose (≤ 50 mg/kg and > 50 mg/kg), gender of animals (male, unspecified, and female), and treatment duration (≤ 10 days and > 10 days) to identify heterogeneity sources. These analyses focused on outcomes frequently reported in the included studies, with P < 0.05 denoting statistical significance. Additionally, sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess the robustness of the findings by sequentially excluding individual studies and evaluating their impact on pooled effect sizes and heterogeneity. These steps aimed to ensure the reliability and transparency of the results. Publication Bias Publication bias was evaluated using Egger’s test for datasets numbering seven or more. If bias was detected, the trimming and filling methods were applied to adjust for asymmetry in the funnel plot. These methods estimate the number of missing studies, impute their potential effect sizes, and recalculate the overall pooled effect. The results, before and after adjustments, were compared to assess the robustness of the findings. Any significant discrepancies were interpreted with caution, as they may indicate potential limitations in the dataset. Time-dose analysis To elucidate the relationship between dose, administration time, and outcomes, three-dimensional (3D) scatter plots and radar maps illustrating the time-dose effect were generated. These studies, published between 2012 and 2024, highlight the growing interest in baicalin’s therapeutic effects on UC. The selection process is depicted in (Fig. 1 ). Characteristics of included studies This study incorporated 17 articles, out of which 15 were conducted in English, involving a total of 781 animals. Within this cohort, 293 were categorized as part of the experimental group, and 151 were in the model group. The animal species utilized included 76 BALB/c mice (9.7%), 193 C57BL/6 mice (24.7%), and 512 Sprague-Dawley rats (65.6%) (Fig. 2 A). Regarding gender specificity (Fig. 2 B), 10 studies exclusively used male animals, 2 focused solely on females, and 4 did not specify the sex of the animals, resulting in males representing 69.7% (544/781), females 9.9% (77/781), and unspecified sex 20.5% (160/781). The use of anaesthetics varied across studies: chloral hydrate in five papers (29.4%), sodium pentobarbital in one (5.9%), ether in two (11.8%), and two papers did not specify the type of anaesthetic used (11.8%). Additionally, 41.2% (7/17) of the literature did not mention the use of anaesthetics (Fig. 2 C). Baicalin dosage ranged from 30 mg/kg to 150 mg/kg administered via gavage, with intervention durations between 7 and 30 days, including 7 studies with long-term administrations (> 10 days, 41.2%) and 10 with short-term administrations (≤ 10 days, 58.8%) (Fig. 2 D).In the study, the experimental group received baicalin treatment, whereas the model group and the blank control were administered solvents(Supplementary Table 3). For UC induction(Fig. 2 F), nine papers employed intrarectal injections of TNBS (52.9%), seven added dextrose sodium sulphate to drinking water (41.2%), and one utilized other methods (5.9%). In assessing baicalin’s efficacy for treating Ulcerative Colitis (UC), we reviewed the relevant literature. Seven studies provided histological scores (HCS); seven detailed changes in body weight; ten assessed the Disease Activity Index (DAI); nine evaluated Colon Length (CL); two measured index of spleen levels; and two examined ZO-1 expression levels. Additionally, a marked infiltration of immune cells, particularly neutrophils and macrophages, was observed in affected tissues. These immune cells play a crucial role in the inflammatory process by releasing pro-inflammatory cytokines and reactive oxygen species, thereby exacerbating tissue injury. Eight histopathological analyses were conducted, among which one study [ 24 ] exclusively utilized Hematoxylin and Eosin (HE) staining. Meta-analysis of seven studies demonstrated that the Histological Score (HCS) in the baicalin (BA) group was significantly reduced compared to the Ulcerative Colitis (UC) model group, ( n = 112, SMD = −3.91, 95% CI: [−4.63, −3.19], p < 0.00001, Fig. 3 A).Heterogeneity testing revealed no substantial variation among studies (χ 2 = 10.58, I 2 = 43%, p = 0.10), prompting the use of a random effects model. Disease Activity Index (DAI) Ten studies employed the DAI as an outcome metric. The analyses revealed that the baicalin (BA) group exhibited significantly reduced DAI levels compared to the Ulcerative Colitis (UC) model group, ( n = 172, MD = −2.75, 95% CI [−3.76,−1.75], p < 0.00001, Fig. 3 B). Heterogeneity testing demonstrated significant variability across studies (χ 2 = 1760.03, I 2 = 99%, p < 0.00001), necessitating the adoption of a random effects model. In addition, the analysis results showed that the baicalin (BA) group could effectively increase the Body Weight Change (BWC) and Colon Length (CL) and decrease the Spleen Index compared with UC model animals group, and the differences were statistically significant (Supplementary Fig. 1). Heterogeneity testing revealed no substantial differences across the studies (χ 2 = 0.07, I 2 = 0%, p = 1.00), leading to the application of a fixed-effects model. Heterogeneity testing indicated considerable variability across the studies (χ 2 = 16.28, I 2 = 88%, p = 0.008), necessitating the use of a random effects model. IL-6 and mRNA levels of IL-6 The results indicated that IL-6 protein levels were significantly elevated in the model group, consistent with the inflammatory nature of ulcerative colitis. Treatment with baicalin effectively reduced IL-6 levels ( n = 94, SMD = −10.59, 95% CI [−15.94,−5.24], p = 0.0001, Supplementary Fig. 3A), demonstrating its anti-inflammatory potential. Similarly, the mRNA levels of IL-6 were also markedly increased in the model group, indicating active transcription and synthesis of this pro-inflammatory cytokine. Baicalin treatment significantly downregulated IL-6 mRNA levels, suggesting its role in modulating transcriptional activity and thereby reducing overall inflammation ( n = 64, MD = −3.32, 95% CI [−4.83,−1.81], p < 0.0001, Supplementary Fig. 4B). The heterogeneity test for IL-6 (χ 2 = 79.94, I 2 = 94%, p < 0.00001) and mRNA levels of IL-6 (χ 2 = 898.09, I 2 = 100%, p < 0.00001) showed a high I 2 value, indicating substantial heterogeneity across studies; hence, a random-effects model was applied to provide a more conservative estimate of the effect size. TNF-α and mRNA levels of TNF-α The levels of TNF-α, another key pro-inflammatory cytokine, were notably increased in the model group, reflecting its role in promoting inflammation and tissue damage. Baicalin administration resulted in a significant decrease in TNF-α levels, indicating its effectiveness in attenuating inflammatory responses ( n = 84, SMD = −8.05, 95% CI [−12.31,−3.78], p = 0.0002, Supplementary Fig. 3B). Correspondingly, the mRNA levels of TNF-α were also elevated in the model group, highlighting increased transcriptional activity. Baicalin treatment led to a substantial reduction in TNF-α mRNA expression, which further supports its regulatory effects on inflammation at both the protein and gene expression levels ( n = 48, SMD = −3.35, 95% CI [−5.50,−1.20], p = 0.002, Supplementary Fig. 5B). Subgroup analyses Given the observed high heterogeneity across studies, we conducted subgroup analyses for ten metrics: HCS(Supplementary Table 4, Supplementary Fig. 10), CL(Supplementary Table 5, Supplementary Fig. 11), NF-κB (Supplementary Table 6, Supplementary Fig. 12) were stratified by species to effectively reduce heterogeneity. None of the indicators effectively reduced heterogeneity through treatment duration stratification. Histological Score (HCS) Significant reductions in heterogeneity were observed in C57BL/6 mice, while high heterogeneity persisted in Sprague-Dawley rats. BALB/c mice were not analyzed for heterogeneity due to limited data. Similarly, lower heterogeneity was noted in male subjects, with insufficient data for female and unreported genders. Short treatment durations (≤ 10 days) and lower doses (≤ 50 mg/kg) also exhibited reduced heterogeneity, indicating that species, gender, treatment duration, and dosage significantly influence HCS outcomes. The results are presented in Supplementary Table 4. Colon Length (CL) C57BL/6 mice and BALB/c mice showed decreased heterogeneity, unlike Sprague-Dawley rats, which maintained high heterogeneity levels. Gender analysis revealed lower heterogeneity in studies not specifying animal sex, with higher levels observed in male subjects. Both short and long treatment durations exhibited high heterogeneity, suggesting treatment length does not significantly impact CL heterogeneity. However, higher doses (> 50 mg/kg) showed reduced heterogeneity, pointing to dosage as a potential source of variation. Detailed results of the subgroup analyses are shown in Supplementary Table 5. Potential mechanisms of action The mechanisms underlying baicalin’s (BA) efficacy in treating Ulcerative Colitis (UC) are diverse, intricate, and target multiple pathways. A detailed overview of these mechanisms is provided in (Supplementary Table 15). Time-Dose interval analyses In patients with Ulcerative Colitis (UC), there is a positive correlation between the Disease Activity Index (DAI) [ 34 ] and Histological Score (HCS) [ 35 ] with disease severity, while Body Weight Change (BWC) and Colon Length (CL) are inversely correlated [ 36 , 37 ]. Elevated levels of Myeloperoxidase (MPO) [ 38 ], as well as TNF-α and IL-1β in feces [ 39 ], and TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 in both serum [ 39 , 40 ] and mucosa [ 41 , 42 ], are indicative of UC severity. These biomarkers are essential for the diagnosis and evaluation of UC. In this study, these indicators were employed to assess the time-dose impact of baicalin on UC. Through the generation of three-dimensional (3D) images reflecting dose and time effects, alongside dose-response radargrams, we aimed to identify the optimal treatment duration and the most effective baicalin dosage (Supplementary Tables 16–23). Baicalin (BA) demonstrated efficacy in reducing Disease Activity Index (DAI) levels across a dosage range of 25 mg/kg to 150 mg/kg in all examined conditions ( n = 17), suggesting that this dose range is optimal for UC treatment. Specifically, 3D scatter plots indicated a significant reduction in DAI levels within 7 to 30 days of treatment (Figs. 4 A and 5 A). Fig. 4 Scatter plot of the time-dose interval analysis on A DAI, B BWC, C CL and (D) HCS Fig. 5 Radar map of the time-dose interval analysis on A DAI, B BWC, C CL and (D) HCS In terms of Body Weight Change (BWC), BA increased levels at doses of 100 mg/kg to 150 mg/kg ( n = 9). However, at lower doses of 25 mg/kg to 50 mg/kg( n = 6), 83.3% ( n = 5) of cases showed effectiveness, while 16.7% ( n = 1) did not, indicating a higher efficacy at 100 mg/kg to 150 mg/kg. The 3D scatter plots corroborated that BWC levels improved significantly within the same 7 to 30-day period (Figs. 4 B, 5 C). For Colon Length (CL), BA was effective across all cases at doses between 60 mg/kg and 150 mg/kg ( n = 8). A lower efficacy was observed at 25 mg/kg to 50 mg/kg ( n = 6), with 83.3% ( n = 5) effectiveness, suggesting that higher doses are preferable for UC treatment. The data also showed BA’s enhanced effectiveness in increasing CL beyond 7 days of intervention (Figs. 4 C, 5 C). Regarding Histological Score (HCS), BA at 100 mg/kg to 120 mg/kg ( n = 4) reduced levels in all conditions, contrasting with lower efficacy at 25 mg/kg to 50 mg/kg ( n = 7), where 85.7% ( n = 6) were effective. This suggests that doses between 100 mg/kg and 120 mg/kg are more beneficial, with the most significant reduction in HCS observed between 7 and 14 days (Figs. 4 D and 5 D). For Myeloperoxidase (MPO) levels, BA was effective at 60 mg/kg to 150 mg/kg ( n = 4), while a 50% ( n = 2) effectiveness was noted at 30 mg/kg to 50 mg/kg, indicating that higher doses are more advantageous. The therapeutic effect was more pronounced during 14 to 30 days compared to shorter durations(Supplementary Fig. 23A, 24 A). In the case of TNF-α, a higher effectiveness was noted at 60 mg/kg to 100 mg/kg ( n = 3), with lower doses showing less efficacy. Long-term interventions yielded better TNF-α reduction compared to shorter durations (Supplementary Fig. 23B, 24B). For IL-6, BA effectively reduced levels at 30 mg/kg to 100 mg/kg ( n = 4), particularly during 7 to 14 days of intervention(Supplementary Fig. 20 C, 21 C). Similarly, IL-1β levels decreased significantly at doses of 60 mg/kg to 100 mg/kg ( n = 4), with the most effective period being 10 to 14 days (Supplementary Fig. 23D, 24D). Collectively, these results suggest that baicalin, administered at 60–150 mg/kg over 10–14 days, offers superior efficacy in treating UC. Scutellaria baicalensis Georgi, utilized in traditional Chinese medicine for ulcerative colitis (UC) treatment, contains baicalin as its primary active component. The herb is categorized based on its age: Scutellaria baicalensis Georgi (≤ 2 years) and Scutellaria baicalensis Georgi (> 2 years). Notably, baicalin content in Scutellaria baicalensis Georgi diminishes as the plant ages beyond two years [ 43 ]. Hence, for UC treatment, Scutellaria baicalensis Georgi aged two years or less is recommended, aligning with the traditional Chinese medicinal principle that it is particularly beneficial for conditions affecting the ‘middle and lower jiao.’ Among the various parts of the plant, the root is richest in baicalin, making it the most effective and cost-efficient for clinical use in UC management [ 44 ]. In terms of dosage, based on the human-mouse conversion theory [ 45 ], the equivalent human dosage ranges from 4.12 to 10.29 g for rats and 2.08–5.19 g for mice. Consequently, a dosage range of 4.12–5.19 g is deemed optimal and practical for UC treatment. This range suggests a potentially optimal and reasonable dosage for clinical application in UC management. The formula is presented in (Supplementary formula.1 A, 1B). Discussion Summary This study aimed to elucidate the protective effects and underlying mechanisms of baicalin in animal models of Ulcerative Colitis (UC). Through a comprehensive meta-analysis of 17 papers involving 781 animals, our findings indicate that baicalin significantly ameliorates oxidative stress markers, inflammatory markers, UC phenotype scores, and apoptosis indices. These outcomes suggest baicalin’s pronounced protective effect in experimental UC models, potentially through modulating inflammatory responses, enhancing anti-apoptotic pathways, and mitigating oxidative stress. The lack of a statistically significant effect of baicalin on IL-17 mRNA levels may be attributed to variations in experimental animal species and limited sample sizes. To address this, future studies should consider using alternative animal models, such as genetically modified mice with enhanced IL-17 expression, to better simulate UC pathogenesis. Additionally, optimizing experimental protocols to reduce variability-such as standardizing diet and housing conditions-may help uncover subtle effects. Finally, exploring a broader range of baicalin dosages could provide insights into potential dose-dependent effects on IL-17 mRNA levels, thereby strengthening the mechanistic understanding of baicalin’s role in UC treatment. Subgroup analyses for several metrics revealed potential sources of heterogeneity, including species and treatment dose for CL, species, gender, treatment duration, and dose for HCS, and gender for TNF-α heterogeneity. The origins of heterogeneity for DAI, IL-10 mRNA, and SOD remain unidentified. This may be due to variations in experimental protocols, such as differences in dosing regimens, animal models, and outcome measurement techniques. Additionally, the methodological quality of included studies varies, with some studies lacking details on randomization and blinding, which could contribute to unexplained variability. Future studies should adopt standardized protocols and higher methodological rigor to reduce heterogeneity. Moreover, subgroup analyses focusing on potential confounding factors, such as animal strain differences and intervention durations, could provide further insights into the sources of variability. Publication bias assessment for four metrics revealed bias only in HCS. However, subsequent trim-and-fill analyses did not qualitatively alter the outcome, underscoring the results’ robustness. Time-dose interval analysis identified 60–150 mg/kg of baicalin over 10–14 weeks as the most effective range, suggesting optimal conditions for UC treatment in animal models. Notably, the study’s scope was confined to mouse models, limiting our ability to extrapolate these protective effects to other animal models or to clinical settings. The relatively small sample size also necessitates cautious interpretation of the findings, emphasizing the need for further research to refine our understanding and provide more definitive evidence. Potential mechanisms of action Ulcerative Colitis (UC) is characterized by chronic inflammation of the rectum and colon, attributed to compromised intestinal epithelial barriers, dysregulated immune responses, and dysbiosis [ 46 – 48 ]. Our study utilized DSS and TNBS-induced UC models to explore baicalin’s therapeutic mechanisms. DSS induces UC through the formation of nanolipid vesicles that increase colonic membrane permeability and inflammatory factor levels (e.g., IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α) [ 49 , 50 ]. Conversely, TNBS-induced UC is driven by ethanol-mediated mucosal barrier breakdown, leading to heightened IFN-γ secretion by CD4 + T cells [ 51 , 52 ]. The findings from the analyzed studies indicate that baicalin’s protective effects in Ulcerative Colitis (UC) are multifaceted. The potential mechanisms through which baicalin exerts its therapeutic benefits in UC are outlined below. Anti-inflammatory Mechanisms The pathogenesis of UC is intimately linked to intestinal inflammation, wherein dendritic cells and macrophages play pivotal roles in mediating immune tolerance and T cell differentiation [ 53 ]. An imbalance between effector T helper (Th) cells and regulatory T cells (Tregs) precipitates abnormal cytokine production, with TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-17, IFN-γ, and ROR-γt serving as key inflammatory mediators [ 54 ]. Baicalin’s protective effects in UC are multifaceted, encompassing: Regulation of Macrophage Activity: Baicalin downregulates macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF), the number of macrophages (MΦs), and macrophage-related cytokines (e.g., MCP-1, MIP-3α), suggesting its role in modulating macrophage-mediated inflammatory responses. NF-κB Pathway Modulation: The transcription factor NF-κB, pivotal in inflammatory signaling, is regulated by baicalin through the inhibition of NF-κB p65 subunit phosphorylation, thereby attenuating pro-inflammatory gene expression [ 55 ]. T Cell Balance Restoration: Baicalin appears to restore the balance between regulatory and effector T cells, reducing the proliferation of pathogenic Th17 cells while promoting Treg cell activity, crucial for maintaining intestinal immune homeostasis [ 56 ]. Inhibition of Pro-inflammatory Cytokines: Toll-like receptors (TLRs) are pivotal transmembrane proteins involved in recognizing microbial pathogens and crucial in upholding the intestinal epithelial barrier’s integrity [ 57 ]. Through the suppression of the TLR4/NF-κB-p65/IL-6 signaling pathway and the downregulation of TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-13 mRNA expression [ 58 , 59 ], baicalin effectively reduces serum levels of key inflammatory markers, including IL-1β, IL-17, and IL-6 [ 60 ]. (2) Antioxidant Action Oxidative stress plays a pivotal role in the pathogenesis of UC, with the body’s exogenous antioxidant defense system, including Superoxide Dismutase (SOD) and other enzymatic antioxidants, combating this stress [ 61 ]. Malondialdehyde (MDA), a byproduct of lipid peroxidation, serves as a primary indicator of cellular oxidative damage. Our findings indicate that baicalin enhances the expression of SOD, contributing to the antioxidant defense, and concurrently reduces MDA levels, thereby mitigating oxidative damage in UC [ 62 ]. (3) Anti-apoptotic Effects Apoptosis, or programmed cell death, is a critical process in the perpetuation of UC. The caspase-9/PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, particularly sensitive to microenvironmental changes such as DNA damage and ROS accumulation, initiates caspase-9-dependent apoptosis. The inhibition of caspase-9, therefore, represents a strategic target to curb apoptosis Furthermore, the Fas/FasL system and B-cell lymphoma 2 (BCL-2) family proteins, which regulate mitochondrial apoptosis and mitochondrial outer membrane permeability (MOMP), are central to the apoptotic process. Our analysis suggests that baicalin attenuates TNBS-induced intestinal mucosa cell apoptosis by inhibiting the PI3K/AKT pathway activation, reducing caspase-3, 9, and BAX production, and enhancing Bcl-2 expression in the colonic mucosa. The inhibition of apoptosis is crucial in the management of Ulcerative Colitis (UC). The caspase-9/PI3K/AKT pathway, notably caspase-9-dependent apoptosis, responds to various microenvironmental stressors such as DNA damage, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and withdrawal of growth factors [ 63 , 64 ]. Inhibiting caspase-9 curtails apoptosis [ 65 ], while the activation and phosphorylation of the PI3K/AKT pathway significantly influence caspase-9 and the Bcl-2/Bax protein expressions [ 66 , 67 ]. The Fas/FasL system is instrumental in initiating apoptosis, where Fas binds to FasL-expressing cells [ 68 ], triggering a cascade that forms a death-inducing signaling complex with Fas/FADD/Procaspase-8/−10. This complex activates caspase-8/−10, which in turn activates caspase-3/−6/−7, leading to apoptosis. Furthermore, the B-cell lymphoma 2 (BCL-2) family of proteins modulates mitochondrial apoptosis by regulating the mitochondrial outer membrane’s permeability, subsequently activating the caspases involved in apoptosis execution [ 69 ]. Additionally, the release of BAX (Bcl-2-associated X protein) is known to facilitate apoptosis [ 70 ]. Our findings indicate that baicalin (BA) can mitigate TNBS-induced apoptosis in intestinal mucosa cells by inhibiting the PI3K/AKT pathway’s activation, reducing caspase-3, −9, and BAX production, and enhancing Bcl-2 levels in the colonic mucosa. (4) Intestinal Barrier Repair The integrity of the intestinal mucosal barrier is crucial for preventing UC exacerbation, with breaches in this barrier facilitating the invasion of pathogens and exacerbating inflammation [ 71 ]. Tight junctions, particularly those involving Zonula Occludens 1 (ZO-1), form a critical component of the intestinal barrier by sealing spaces between epithelial cells. Baicalin has been shown to bolster the intestinal barrier’s integrity by upregulating ZO-1 expression, thus contributing to the amelioration of UC. Baicalin enhances intestinal barrier integrity, partly through its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. It modulates the TLR4-dependent PI3K/AKT/NF-κB signaling pathway, crucial for epithelial barrier function, and positively influences the intestinal microbiota composition [ 72 ]. This comprehensive action profile underscores baicalin’s potential as a therapeutic agent in UC, targeting both the underlying pathogenic mechanisms and the symptomatic inflammatory responses. Safety of baicalin use Dose/time-response analyses indicate a positive correlation between the dosage and duration of baicalin (BA) administration and its therapeutic effectiveness, with higher doses and longer treatment periods linked to increased efficacy. However, as a bitter-cold drug within the framework of traditional Chinese medicine, specifically the ‘Ku Han Bai Wei’ theory, baicalin’s long-term or high-dose use may pose risks. Research has demonstrated that such usage can disrupt the gastrointestinal mucosal barrier, alter gastrointestinal hormone secretion, affect gastrointestinal motility, and disturb the intestinal flora [ 73 ]. Therefore, it is essential to thoroughly investigate baicalin’s safety profile to ensure that its therapeutic benefits are maximized without compromising patient health. Numerous randomized, double-blind clinical trials have highlighted baicalin’s favorable safety profile [ 13 , 74 – 76 ]. However, these studies often involved baicalin in combination with other drugs or as a primary component of complex formulations, indicating that further research is necessary to isolate and understand baicalin’s safety when used independently. Among the 17 papers reviewed, only two addressed the absence of baicalin’s toxic side effects on cellular models, leaving room for a more comprehensive assessment of its safety. Research indicates that a dose of 2000 mg/kg is considered safe for rats, with no significant toxicological effects reported [ 11 ]. While a dose of 2000 mg/kg was deemed safe for rats, translating this dose to humans requires consideration of interspecies differences in metabolism and pharmacokinetics. Using the standard human equivalent dose (HED), HED (mg/kg) = Animal dose (mg/kg) × (Animal weight/Human weight)^(1/3), the equivalent dose for a 60 kg human would be approximately 324 mg/kg, or 19.4 g/day. This calculation highlights the importance of dose optimization in clinical trials, as safety and efficacy thresholds for humans may differ significantly from those in animal studies. Further pharmacokinetic studies are necessary to refine these estimations and guide clinical applications. Nevertheless, concerns have been raised regarding high baicalin consumption, such as potential weight loss and decreased trace mineral levels, which could impair the function of metalloenzyme-containing enzymes and lead to adverse health consequences [ 77 ]. Despite these findings, such adverse effects have not been corroborated in clinical trials, suggesting baicalin’s safety and low toxicity profile in both animal models and humans, with a minimal risk of adverse effects. Regarding the possibility of grouping doses utilized in the studies, we recognize that this could enhance our understanding of the dose-response relationship and inform dosing recommendations. Grouping doses could provide insights into therapeutic windows and help identify not only effective doses but also those that minimize safety risks. However, our analysis faced several challenges that limited our ability to group doses effectively. The doses reported in the included studies varied considerably, and the number of studies within each dose group was often insufficient to draw meaningful conclusions. Additionally, grouping doses would require subjective decisions about which doses to include in each category, potentially introducing bias into our findings. Despite these challenges, we are committed to further exploring the safety and efficacy of baicalin. Future research should focus on well-designed clinical trials that assess the safety profile of baicalin at various dosages. Additionally, further investigations into the optimal dosing strategies could help clarify the therapeutic potential of baicalin while ensuring patient safety. Addressing baicalin’s low bioavailability and poor water solubility remains critical for enhancing its clinical application. Advanced delivery systems, including phospholipid vesicles, nanoliposomes, lipid nanocapsules, polymeric nanocapsules, nanoparticles, nanosponges, and nanoemulsions [ 78 – 84 ], have shown promise in improving baicalin’s local bioavailability, cellular uptake, and therapeutic efficacy through synergistic mechanisms [ 85 – 87 ]. Future prospects The therapeutic efficacy of baicalin in UC and its underlying mechanisms, as demonstrated in animal studies, necessitates further validation in more diverse and extensive research settings. Specifically, experiments involving higher dosages and prolonged treatment durations are essential for establishing a solid foundation for subsequent clinical trials in humans. Moreover, the advent of nanotechnology presents an opportunity to overcome baicalin’s pharmacokinetic limitations, potentially revolutionizing its delivery and enhancing its bioavailability and synergistic effects. Further research is necessary to explore optimal dosages and ensure safety when baicalin is applied to humans. In addition, safety or toxicity assessments, along with an acknowledgment of experimental limitations, are recommended to enrich future research in this field. Limitations This systematic review of animal experiments on baicalin’s effects in Ulcerative Colitis (UC) encounters several limitations: Language Bias: The language scope was limited to Chinese and English, potentially excluding relevant studies published in other languages. This introduces a selection bias that could skew the findings toward regions where these languages dominate academic publishing. For example, studies conducted in non-English-speaking European countries or regions with high UC prevalence may provide additional insights into baicalin’s efficacy. To enhance generalizability, future meta-analyses should aim to include studies from a broader linguistic range by incorporating translation tools and international collaborations. Quality of Studies: According to the SYRCLE risk of bias tool, the included randomized controlled trials exhibited varying levels of quality, with several studies demonstrating unclear or significant biases in critical areas such as blinding and allocation concealment. These limitations raise concerns about the authenticity and generalizability of the findings. The presence of such biases may affect the overall reliability of the results and limit our ability to draw definitive conclusions regarding the efficacy of baicalin in treating ulcerative colitis. Publication Bias: Although Egger’s test for publication bias was performed and indicated that the majority of measures showed little bias, the selection of studies may still have introduced biases into the meta-analysis outcomes. The inherent tendency to publish positive results could affect the overall interpretation of the efficacy of baicalin, leading to potential overestimations of its therapeutic effects on ulcerative colitis. Therefore, while our findings are promising, they should be interpreted with caution, and further research is warranted to confirm these results in a more unbiased context. Heterogeneity: While significant heterogeneity was assessed using the Chi-square and I² tests, and subgroup analyses based on factors such as animal species and dosage helped reduce heterogeneity in some instances, the sources of heterogeneity remained largely unexplored in most studies. This persistence of unexplained variability is likely attributable to methodological differences, variations in study design, and discrepancies in dosing regimens and outcome measures. As a result, caution should be exercised in interpreting the findings, as the unexplained heterogeneity may influence the overall conclusions regarding the efficacy of baicalin in treating ulcerative colitis. Ethical Review: The absence of ethical review mentions in some studies questions the integrity of the experimental designs. Species Specificity: A significant limitation of this study is the exclusive reliance on animal models to assess the impact of baicalin on ulcerative colitis. While these models provide valuable insights into the drug’s mechanisms and potential efficacy, the findings may not be directly applicable to human populations due to differences in physiology and disease manifestation. Therefore, clinical studies are essential to verify the effectiveness and safety of baicalin in humans before any clinical recommendations can be made. Adverse Effects: A lack of adverse effect reporting in the literature leaves a gap in understanding baicalin’s safety profile. Literature Scope: The limited number of studies included may skew the conclusions drawn from the meta-analysis. Incomplete Experimental Protocols: Specific details about the experimental protocols used in the included studies, such as how control groups were created and how optimal dosages were calculated, were often lacking. This absence of critical methodological information impacts reproducibility and the capacity to validate results, making it challenging to draw definitive conclusions regarding baicalin’s effectiveness. Further safety or toxicity assessments and acknowledgment of experimental limitations are recommended to enrich future research in this field. Conclusion This meta-analysis comprehensively assessed the efficacy and safety of baicalin in treating ulcerative colitis (UC). Baicalin demonstrated significant influence on crucial biomarkers linked to UC, such as Disease Activity Index (DAI), Histological Score (HCS), Body Weight Change (BWC), Colon Length (CL), and inflammatory markers including TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β. These effects are attributed to baicalin’s anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, anti-apoptotic properties, and its ability to enhance intestinal barrier repair, potentially through the modulation of pathways like PI3K/AKT, TLR4/NF-κB, IKK/IKB, TLRs/MyD88, Bcl-2/Bax, Th17/Treg, and TLRs/MyD88. Our findings indicate a dose-dependent and time-dependent therapeutic action of baicalin, with an optimal dose range of 60–150 mg/kg and a treatment duration of 10–14 days being suggested. Despite its benefits, baicalin’s bitter-cold nature, as per traditional Chinese medicine, raises concerns regarding its long-term or high-dose use and its potential gastrointestinal side effects. The review highlights specific adverse effects observed in the included studies. Gastrointestinal issues such as diarrhea and mucosal damage were reported in high-dose treatments. Hormone disruptions, including altered cortisol levels, were noted in animal models subjected to prolonged baicalin exposure. Additionally, intestinal flora disturbances included significant reductions in beneficial bacterial populations such as Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium. These examples provide a clearer context for the potential risks associated with baicalin usage, supported by references to studies [ 88 ]. Consequently, while baicalin presents a viable option for UC management, it is crucial to consider its therapeutic advantages against potential safety risks. Future research, especially clinical trials, is imperative to ascertain the ideal dosing and treatment duration to optimize baicalin’s benefits while mitigating adverse effects, aiming to establish a detailed safety profile for extended use. In summary, baicalin offers a significant contribution to UC treatment, supported by both traditional Chinese medicine and contemporary pharmacological research. Upcoming studies should prioritize optimizing treatment protocols and ensuring patient safety, thereby unlocking baicalin’s full therapeutic potential in UC management. documents.title: Diagnostic delay in adult inflammatory bowel disease: A systematic review.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The extent of diagnostic delay in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is incompletely understood. We aimed to understand the extent of diagnostic delay of IBD in adults and identify associations between patient or healthcare characteristics and length of delay.
METHODS: Articles were sourced from EMBASE, Medline and CINAHL from inception to April 2021. Inclusion criteria were adult cohorts (18 ≥ years old) reporting median time periods between onset of symptoms for Crohn's disease (CD), ulcerative colitis (UC) or IBD (i.e. CD and UC together) and a final diagnosis (diagnostic delay). Narrative synthesis was used to examine the extent of diagnostic delay and characteristics associated with delay. Sensitivity analysis was applied by the removal of outliers.
RESULTS: Thirty-one articles reporting median diagnostic delay for IBD, CD or UC were included. After sensitivity analysis, the majority of IBD studies (7 of 8) reported a median delay of between 2 and 5.3 months. From the studies examining median delay in UC, three-quarters (12 of 16) reported a delay between 2 and 6 months. In contrast, three-quarters of the CD studies (17 of 23) reported a delay of between 2 and 12 months. No characteristic had been examined enough to understand their role in diagnostic delay in these populations.
CONCLUSIONS: This systematic review provides robust insight into the extent of diagnostic delay in IBD and suggests further intervention is needed to reduce delay in CD particularly. Furthermore, our findings provide a benchmark value range for diagnostic delay, which such future work can be measured against.

Bullet points of the study highlights What is already known? Diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)﻿ is frequently delayed. Reported extent of delay is varied, ranging from a few months to several years. It remains unclear whether certain patient groups are more vulnerable to delay. What is new in this study? The provisions of tighter benchmarks of the extent of diagnostic delay in IBD. Examination of the role of specific characteristics (disease type, age of onset) on diagnostic delay of IBD. What are the future clinical and research implications of the study findings? Impact of newer diagnostic tests like fecal calprotectin on the delay in IBD diagnosis. More research is required into the role of patient characteristics on the extent of diagnostic delay. Introduction Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic inflammatory condition affecting the gastrointestinal tract, the most prevalent examples being Crohn’s disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC) [ 1 ]. Approximately 6.8 million cases of IBD were reported globally in 2017, with nearly a quarter of these cases in North America, resulting in a significant personal and societal burden [ 2 ]. The clinical presentation of IBD is variable, but can include change in bowel habit, rectal bleeding, fatigue and weight loss [ 3 ]. In addition, approximately 25% to 40% of individuals with IBD display extraintestinal manifestations, which include arthritis, axial spondyloarthritis, uveitis, erythema nodosum and primary sclerosing cholangitis [ 4 ]. The range of such presenting symptoms can make it challenging for clinicians to promptly identify patients with IBD, and symptoms can be attributed to other conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome, all of which can lead to diagnostic delay [ 5 ]. Such delays may be further contributed to by factors such as patient demographics, geographical location and the presence of extraintestinal manifestations [ 6 – 9 ]. For example, in affected countries, symptoms of IBD may be mistaken for abdominal tuberculosis [ 10 ]. In cases of diagnostic delay, adverse impacts on clinical outcomes can occur, including an increased need for subsequent surgical intervention and poor response to medical therapy [ 11 , 12 ]. Recent reports suggest the average diagnostic delay of IBD can range anywhere from 2 months to 8 years [ 5 , 13 ] and that delays in the diagnosis of CD are longer than for UC [ 6 , 12 , 14 ]. This wide variation reported in the differences in the delay experienced by patients, means the true extent of the problem of delay remains unclear. The aim of this systematic review was to provide a clearer benchmark range for the extent of diagnostic delay, as well as providing information on any characteristics that may be associated with delay. Methods Data sources and searches We conducted a systematic review by searching the medical literature databases of Medline, EMBASE and CINAHL from their inception to April 2021, using a combination of free-text and medical subject headings (MeSH) terms, or equivalents from each database (Supplementary Table 1 ). Search terms were devised for IBD and diagnostic delay using existing systematic reviews that explored other aspects of IBD, and reviews investigating diagnostic delay in other long-term conditions [ 15 – 17 ]. Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines were followed during the completion of this systematic review and the protocol was logged with International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) (registration number: CRD42018108886). Study selection The inclusion criteria were developed using the Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcomes and Study (PICOS) framework [ 18 ]. The included populations were adults aged 18 years or older with a confirmed diagnosis of IBD, CD or UC. Studies with adult populations which included a proportion of participants under 18 years old were retained if the mean age implied the population was largely formed from participants above 18 years old. Studies also had to include the primary outcome of interest, a reported average time period of diagnostic delay for IBD, CD or UC from symptom onset to final diagnosis. Studies were excluded if they examined delay, but did not report data related to the extent of, or a characteristic related to, the time period of diagnostic delay (i.e. defined as wrong outcomes) or their design included case studies or case series with less than ten participants, literature reviews, systematic reviews or conference abstracts. There were no restrictions on time of publication, as databases were searched from inception. Articles in languages other than English were included, individuals who spoke the language were then requested to make initial assessments and then, if necessary, quality appraise and extract pertinent data, with Google Translate also being used if necessary. Once the database searches had been undertaken using the reported criteria, the reference manager software Mendeley was used to remove duplicates (Version 1.16.1, Mendeley Ltd., London, UK). The authors E. C. and J. A. P. then completed an independent title and abstract review of 50% of the initially identified articles each. Articles that progressed to abstract review underwent a second review, where E. C. reviewed the abstracts initially reviewed by J. A. P. and vice versa. These included abstracts then underwent a full-text review, with E. C. independently reviewing all full texts and the remaining three authors (J. A. P., B. S., A. D. F.) reviewing a proportion of full texts each. Throughout the review process, disagreements between reviewers were resolved through discussion and by consulting an arbitrating author (BS). Data extraction and analysis Data extraction of included articles was completed by two reviewers (E. C., J. A. P.). The primary outcome of interest extracted was the reported average time period of diagnostic delay of IBD (for articles that did not distinguish between CD and UC), CD or UC, from symptom onset to diagnosis. Average data regarding diagnostic delay could be reported as mean or median values, with both being recorded along with their accompanying estimate of accuracy (standard deviation or interquartile range respectively). However, due to the typical non-normality of mean diagnostic delay data, only median values were used in this analysis [ 19 ]. This allowed for data which was more representative of the average delay actually experienced by patient samples, though removed the possibility to pool data from all included articles using meta-analysis techniques. The unit of time that articles used to report diagnostic delay varied from days to years; therefore, delay data were converted into months to allow comparability of the data. Additional data extracted included lead author, year of publication, time period of participant recruitment, gender, country and mean sample age. Finally, information (where reported) on any specific characteristics (e.g. demographics, symptoms) and their association with reported diagnostic delay were identified in the articles and extracted. Regarding this characteristic data, no restriction was placed on the measure of central tendency here, but rather the focus was on whether differences in delay were experienced across comparator samples (i.e. extent of diagnostic delay in males vs. females). The data from the included articles were examined using narrative synthesis. In the instance of outlier data, sensitivity analysis was performed, resulting in the exclusion of related studies. Quality appraisal A modified Newcastle–Ottawa Score (NOS) was used for quality appraising the included articles, carried out by E. C. and J. A. P. An adapted version of the NOS for cohort studies and for cross-sectional studies were used [ 20 ]. The ‘Selection of participants’ and ‘Measurement of outcome’ were the two criteria of the NOS used to assess quality of articles. The representativeness of studies was assessed based on the geographical spread of recruitment, as well as variation in population characteristics. Results Search results A total of 10,119 unique articles were identified from the three selected databases and underwent title review. Following the exclusion of 6746 articles based upon title, 3373 articles underwent abstract review. From these, 429 articles were reviewed in full, leaving a final 31 articles that reported median data to be included for narrative synthesis (see PRISMA flowchart, below [Fig. 1 ]). Fig. 1 Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) flowchart of the screening process used to identify the included articles Study characteristics Of the 31 articles included in the review, 23 were cohort studies, of which 12 were retrospective [ 6 , 12 – 14 , 21 – 28 ], eight were prospective cohorts [ 9 , 29 – 35 ] and three combined both methods [ 36 – 38 ]. Eight articles used a cross-sectional study design [ 5 , 7 , 8 , 11 , 39 – 42 ]. Nineteen studies were conducted in Europe, seven in Asia, four in North America and one in South America. Twenty articles were based in primary or secondary care, four in tertiary care and five from population registries. Two articles did not report the source from which the sample was drawn. The majority of articles typically documented the criteria used to diagnose IBD in participants, as a combination of clinical features, radiologic and histologic findings. Formal diagnostic criteria used by articles included Lennard–Jones, European Crohn’s and Colitis Organization (ECCO) and Copenhagen diagnostic criteria. Nine articles did not outline the use of any diagnostic criteria. The characteristics of each study included in the review have been summarized in Table 1 . Burgmann et al. [ 5 ] reported median delays of approximately 60–75 months longer than the next closest study across the three analyses. After exclusion of this outlier, the median diagnostic delay of IBD across the remaining eight articles ranged from 2 to 13 months, with three-quarters of these reporting a delay of between 2–5.3 months. Of the 23 studies defining samples solely by CD, the overall delay ranged from 2 to 26.4 months, with three-quarters of the reported median delays ranging from 2 to 12 months. Finally, from the 16 studies examining UC, median diagnostic delay ranged from 2 to 55.2 months, with three-quarter of studies reporting delay between 2 to 6 months. This overall longer median delay observed in patients with CD compared to UC was also mirrored in the subset of studies where delay had been directly compared between the two conditions within the same populations [ 5 , 7 , 13 , 21 , 23 , 34 ]. Finally, when data for each disease category was arranged by year of publication, the extent of delay remained relatively consistent over time from 2009 to 2021 for IBD and UC. However, for the same time period, CD publications showed greater fluctuations year-on-year in reported extent of delay. Factors associated with diagnostic delay Three studies compared differences in delay related to help-seeking (from symptom onset to primary health care consultation) and that which occurred after the first consultation. Though Vavricka found that delay was significantly greater for CD than UC patients during the help-seeking and first consultation phase, Nguyen only found delay after first consultation to final diagnosis to be significantly greater for CD patients compared to UC patients [ 6 , 14 ]. Walker et al. [ 28 ] reported longer delays across help-seeking, primary care and secondary care in CD over UC (Table 3 ). Three articles found statistical significance between increasing age and longer diagnostic delay [ 8 , 25 , 30 ]. The study by Foxworthy and Wilson was the only one that reported median values, showing a statistically significant difference in diagnostic delay of CD between patients over 60 (diagnostic delay 16 months) and patients less than 60 years old at diagnosis (diagnostic delay 5 months) [ 30 ]. In particular, delay is prolonged in patients with CD compared to UC, with the majority of previous studies reporting diagnostic delay less than 12 months for CD, but less than 6 months for UC. Ultimately, these more specific median delay data ranges provide a new benchmark against which interventions to reduce delay in patients with IBD can be compared. However, research examining the specific factors contributing to delay in IBD remains limited and requires further examination to determine any consistent influence. The skewed nature of diagnostic delay data means that (for the majority) of patients with CD diagnosis is achieved within a year of symptom onset, with three-quarter of patients with UC diagnosed in < 6 months. However, across CD studies in particular, there remains a substantial proportion (one in four studies) where on average, receiving a final diagnosis of CD could take between 12 to 24 months from the initial onset of symptoms. These findings provide a more accurate understanding of the true extent of diagnostic delay and though not intended to minimise the problem of diagnostic delay in UC, the greatest impact in a reduction in delay for patients with IBD may come from focusing on CD. Though some degree of interval time period between symptom onset and final diagnosis is inevitable and each country must work within its own practical parameters, we believe that delays of less than 6 months or 12 months for all, not just the majority of, UC and CD patients respectively should be strived for. This should certainly be the case for more advanced healthcare systems, such as the UK, where there remains a minority of patients at the extremes who experience excessive delay, as represented by the interquartile ranges (IQR) by Walker et al. (CD 7.6 months median delay [IQR 3.1–15.0]; UC 3.3 months [1.9–7.3]) [ 28 ]. Our reported findings are based on the studies included in the sensitivity analysis, rather than all identified studies. By removing the study by Burgmann et al. [ 5 ] which reported extremely protracted delays in IBD, CD and UC diagnosis, we have provided a more representative median range for diagnostic delay. Though removal of such outliers is a somewhat arbitrary one, performing this practical sensitivity analysis enabled us to look at the most common length of delay. To support the removal of studies based on their reported, extreme delay values, we examined the details of the study design, but could not identify any clear reason why their data was drastically different to that of the other studies in the systematic review. However, it was of note that this excluded study reported longer diagnostic delay in UC compared to CD, contrary to other included studies. Possible reasons for UC consistently demonstrating shorter diagnostic delays than CD could be because the location of disease is confined to the large bowel and patients experiencing rectal bleeding may be more likely to present to a doctor [ 7 ]. However, CD delays may be longer due to a lack of clinical suspicion and diagnostic testing, associating common CD symptoms like abdominal pain with other conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome and difficulties in identifying disease that is only present in the small bowel [ 12 , 14 , 40 ]. Though the 26 articles which reported overall diagnostic delay were published between 1971 and 2021, the majority was published after 2006 (80%). For the IBD, CD and UC categories, there was no trend of diagnostic delay over this 15-year time period, though the values for IBD and UC were more consistent from 2009 onwards than for CD. However, inherent variations in country demographics, healthcare systems and study designs make such trends difficult to interpret and studies across multiple years in the same countries are needed to examine changes over time in patient delays. Though overall diagnostic delay in patients with IBD, CD or UC has frequently been reported in the literature, there remains limited data to have examined the role of specific patient or healthcare factors in their impact to the extent of delay experienced. Such sub-analysis has proven useful in other systematic reviews into diagnostic delay, as this provides focus on certain characteristics which could prove to be avenues to reduce delay. For example, a previous systematic review on diagnostic delay in giant cell arteritis found delay was greater in those patients who did not experience cranial symptoms compared to those with cranial symptoms [ 16 ]. However, the most frequently examined characteristic we were able to identify was age, and though these studies found delay to be greater in the older of each dichotomized group, there were only three studies, of which two are nearly 40 years old. More studies, of a consistent and repeated design, are needed to make a stronger case for the role of impact of individual characteristics on the extent of diagnostic delay. Though not reporting the extent of delay associated with a specific characteristic as per our study design, several studies did highlight other characteristics which were considered to have a significant role on delay. Vavricka et al. found that of adults categorized as experiencing ‘longer’ diagnostic delay (CD > 24 months and in UC > 12 months), those aged < 40 years compared to those > 40 years (in contrast to our findings) and who had ileal disease compared colon disease were significantly more likely to experience this prolonged delay [ 6 ]. Novacek et al. found ‘greater age’ at diagnosis to be a risk factor for delayed diagnosis in CD as well as in UC. They also found a higher educational level to be a risk factor in patients with CD, but not in UC [ 7 ]. Finally, Lee et al. [ 12 ] found an association between patients with CD and defined as experiencing ‘long’ diagnostic delay (defined as ≥ 21.4 months and 6.2 months in CD and UC, respectively) and perianal discomfort. The select nature of these samples (e.g. those with ‘long’ delay) make comparison with our own included data difficult. Diagnostic delay has been explored in many other studies for a variety of conditions, including giant cell arteritis, gynecological cancers and tuberculosis [ 16 , 43 , 44 ]. Exploring the extent of diagnostic delay in medical conditions, where delays are common, is important as it provides a backdrop for future research examining the reasons for prolonged diagnostic delay and potentially inform interventions for reducing delays and improving patient care. As prolonged diagnostic delay of IBD appears to increase the likelihood of complicated disease, reducing delays in IBD diagnosis could improve the clinical outcome of patients with the condition [ 12 , 45 ]. The specific use of the fecal calprotectin test was not discussed in the studies of this systematic review. It detects levels of calprotectin within stool as a consequence of neutrophil aggregation to the gastrointestinal tract due to active inflammation like that found in IBD [ 46 ]. Existing research suggests that this is effective at differentiating between organic and functional origins of bowel disease, thus could reduce delays in IBD diagnosis [ 47 , 48 ]. The focus on median data within the analysis in this systematic review is a key strength as it reduces problems related to overestimation of averages typically related to use of means from skewed data, providing a more robust estimate of diagnostic delay. Furthermore, as well as examining IBD overall, this systematic review examined the most common disease sub-categories of UC and CD, and, finally, we did not restrict study inclusion based on language, leading to additional studies being included in the review. A limitation of this study is the variation between individual study designs, for instance differences in participant age, method of IBD diagnosis and country. However, despite the introduction of such heterogeneity, this data also provides a fuller picture of the problem of diagnostic delay in this disease group. In conclusion, this systematic review provides a robust insight into the current extent of diagnostic delay in IBD, indicating that diagnostic delay remains a pertinent issue for patients with IBD, particularly CD, but that the factors which may have a role in delay remain unclear. This systematic review provides a backdrop and benchmark onto which further research can be conducted to reduce the time to IBD diagnosis, particularly exploring knowledge of IBD amongst healthcare professionals and the general population to help reduce overall delay. This future research is particularly important, as reducing diagnostic delay of IBD may improve the clinical course of the disease.
